title: Bhamala and the shape of a Buddhist complex
summary: Bhamala’s cruciform stupa is the centre of a larger Buddhist complex. Excavation evidence connects its distinctive plan to chapels, monastic spaces and a history of continued use.

body.text: Bhamala's main stupa is memorable for its cruciform plan, but its shape becomes more meaningful when the surrounding complex is allowed into the picture. Smaller stupas, image chapels, monastic spaces and later excavation discoveries show that this was not one isolated monument. It was an organised setting for a Buddhist community whose use of the place developed over time.

The Department of Archaeology and Museums locates Bhamala in the hills near Khanpur and describes a square-based stupa with projecting stairways on four sides. The projections produce the characteristic cross-shaped plan. That geometry is more informative than comparisons with distant monuments that merely happen to look similar from above.
A centre with surrounding activities

The federal catalogue records smaller votive stupas and image chapels around the main court, with a monastic complex to the south. These elements establish relationships between a principal devotional focus and other spaces. Their distribution can help explain movement, proximity and differences in scale within the sacred precinct.

The plan should not be imagined as fully visible in one historical instant. Archaeological sites often contain structures from successive phases, and an exposed arrangement can bring those phases together in a way that no original visitor experienced. Establishing which walls and floors belong together requires recorded excavation, not visual symmetry alone.
What renewed excavation changed

Abdul Samad's report on the January–March 2013 field season describes work in the western part of the complex and an extension that drew attention to another phase of occupation. The team used systematic recording of deposits and relationships to begin refining the chronology. Training students and staff formed part of the programme alongside the recovery of objects.

The report records terracotta and stucco sculpture and copper coins provisionally associated with the fourth and fifth centuries CE. It uses these findings to argue for activity extending beyond an earlier, narrowly framed understanding of the site. The important point is not simply that more objects were found; the relationship of finds to deposits changed the historical questions that could be asked.
Form is evidence, not a complete explanation

A cruciform stupa can be compared with other Buddhist architectural forms, but shape alone does not identify every ritual performed there. Likewise, an image chapel provides evidence of a devotional setting without preserving all the words, gestures and people that animated it.

Pakistan submitted Bhamala as a separate Tentative List property in 2026. That nomination-stage recognition should be distinguished from World Heritage inscription, and geographical association with Taxila should not be used casually to redraw another property's boundaries.

For the visitor, a rewarding sequence is to understand the principal stupa's outline, then trace how the surrounding spaces relate to it. Finally, consider the excavation record that places those relationships in time. Bhamala's distinctive form is the beginning of discovery; the wider complex and its stratified evidence make that discovery historically substantial.

title: Butkara I: a stupa built through successive phases
summary: Butkara I preserves repeated enlargement around a continuing sacred centre. Its successive stupa phases show why the history of a monument is not always a story of demolition and replacement.

body.text: At Butkara I in Swat, rebuilding did not simply erase what came before. The great stupa developed through successive enlargements that enclosed earlier forms. Its history is therefore nested within its fabric: a continuing sacred focus received new architectural bodies rather than being repeatedly abandoned for an unrelated monument elsewhere.

Research published in Problems of Chronology in Gandharan Art describes five main building periods, corresponding to the original construction and four subsequent reconstructions of the great stupa. It credits Domenico Faccenna's carefully recorded excavations of 1956–62 with establishing the long sequence. Counting those periods accurately matters; five phases do not mean an original building followed by five additional enlargements.
Continuity made through change

An enlargement can preserve the location and meaning of a monument while changing its size, surface and relationship to nearby structures. This is a different model of continuity from leaving every stone untouched. At Butkara, the earlier centre remained important even as later work transformed its appearance.

The surrounding precinct developed too. The federal archaeological catalogue describes the great stupa among smaller votive stupas, columns and other religious structures, with schist paving and a rectangular water tank on the eastern side. The main monument was part of an accumulating environment rather than a solitary object on an empty platform.

For someone reading the site, this creates a challenge. Features visible beside one another today may belong to different episodes of building. A complete-looking plan can conceal chronological complexity. The excavated relationships between foundations, surfaces and additions are what allow a sequence to be reconstructed.
Materials also changed

The specialist chronology study discusses a shift towards plastic materials and associated techniques during later phases, including the use of stucco in architectural and sculptural work. This should not be reduced to a simple story of artistic decline from stone to something less valuable. Different materials support different processes of modelling, repair and alteration.

The study of a material change asks what was replaced, what was retained and how new work related to existing images. Those questions can reveal practical decisions and changing artistic habits without assuming that every phase had the same resources or intentions.
The image of a stupa

A separate study by Luca Maria Olivieri examines an incised slab from Butkara I showing a tall, towered stupa. Such an object adds another kind of evidence: architecture represented in an image. It should not automatically be treated as an exact portrait of the surviving great stupa, but it can contribute to comparisons across Buddhist visual traditions.

The Department of Archaeology notes that sculptures from Butkara are held in Swat Museum. Moving between site and museum helps reconnect architectural setting with displaced objects. The strongest interpretation keeps the phases visible rather than compressing them into a single construction date. Butkara's enduring identity was made through repeated acts of building, donation, adaptation and care.

title: Mahabat Khan Mosque above the bazaar
summary: Mahabat Khan Mosque belongs to Peshawar’s dense market fabric. Its raised setting, entrances and courtyard explain how a religious complex can create a distinct interior without becoming detached from the city.

body.text: Mahabat Khan Mosque is part of Peshawar's old city rather than a monument placed outside its daily life. Approaching through the market setting, the visitor encounters a change in level and enclosure before reaching the courtyard. That transition is central to the building's character: a distinct religious space remains closely connected to streets, trade and neighbouring structures.

The mosque belongs to the seventeenth-century Mughal period. Its precise construction date is not consistently given in the sources: the federal catalogue supplies one date, while historical research has argued for a later foundation associated with Mahabat Khan's governorship. A broad period is more useful here than presenting a disputed year as settled fact.
An urban complex, not only a prayer hall

Samra Khan's architectural research describes the mosque together with an attached teaching establishment and a sarai. It identifies shops facing the bazaar as part of the historical relationship between the complex and its support. This setting complicates a familiar distinction between sacred monument and commercial city. The two could be spatially and economically connected.

The study describes entrances with vaulted porches on several sides and small rooms around the court used for teaching and accommodation. Different users therefore encountered the complex through different activities. The prayer hall was the principal architectural focus, but it did not exhaust the site's functions.
The courtyard as a clearing

The federal catalogue describes an open courtyard with a central ablution pool and a prayer hall on the west, framed by tall minarets. The arrangement gives the interior a clear orientation. Coming from tighter streets, the court offers a larger field of vision and a pause before the sheltered hall.

This openness should not be mistaken for leftover space. It joins the entrances to the prayer front, accommodates movement and allows surrounding rooms to address a common centre. The tank adds a practical religious function to the composition rather than serving solely as a reflective feature for photographs.

Inside the hall, the catalogue records three low domes and painted floral and geometric decoration. The change from an open court to a covered, decorated interior alters both light and attention. Large forms organise the room; smaller painted elements reward a slower inspection.
Surfaces with a repair history

Khan's study discusses damage associated with the 1898 Peshawar fire and subsequent repair and repainting. The decoration seen today must therefore be understood through a history of maintenance, not described indiscriminately as untouched Mughal work. A repaired surface can still be historically significant, but its date and treatment belong in the interpretation.

For visitors, the surrounding bazaar is part of the experience without making the mosque a stage for street photography. Respect worship, leave entrances clear and follow local guidance. The building's achievement is its ability to create a composed religious interior within a dense urban setting. Its authority comes from that relationship as much as from the familiar silhouette of domes and minarets.

title: Gor Khatri: a place with more than one past
summary: Gor Khatri brings deep archaeological deposits together with a Mughal sarai, religious structures and later civic uses. Its value lies in the coexistence of these layers rather than the recovery of one supposedly pure period.

body.text: Gor Khatri resists the usual habit of giving a monument one dynasty, one function and one date. In Peshawar's old city, a substantial enclosure contains standing architecture while archaeological deposits preserve evidence of earlier occupation below it. Religious associations, travel infrastructure and civic uses have each contributed to the place that survives.

The Department of Archaeology describes a sarai established under Princess Jahan Ara Begum in 1640, known as Jahanabad. Its account identifies major eastern and western gateways, an internal quadrangle and ranges of cells. These features make the enclosure legible as an organised institution for movement and accommodation, not simply an empty court surrounded by walls.
Above ground and below ground

Pakistan's 2026 Tentative List submission emphasises the combination of deep archaeological deposits and a standing architectural complex. The two require different forms of reading. Gateways and room ranges can be examined as built spaces; buried deposits depend on controlled excavation and recorded relationships.

A date assigned to an excavated layer does not automatically date the wall standing above it. Conversely, a later building does not make the earlier occupation beneath it irrelevant. Gor Khatri's significance depends on preserving the connection between these different kinds of evidence without merging them into one undifferentiated claim of antiquity.

The nomination discusses possible earlier religious associations, but possibility should remain distinct from a securely identified structure. A name in a historical account, a tradition of pilgrimage and an excavated foundation do not carry identical evidential weight.
A courtyard with changing purposes

The federal catalogue records religious transformations during the Sikh period, while the newer nomination includes colonial civic reuse and the early-twentieth-century fire brigade building. These later elements are not merely clutter obscuring the Mughal sarai. They form part of the history through which the complex remained connected to the city.

This does not mean every alteration must be valued equally or that conservation requires retaining every recent addition. It means decisions should begin with documentation and an understanding of significance. Restoring an imagined single-period appearance can erase evidence that helps explain how an urban place survived.
A place where heritage work happens

The Heritage Foundation of Pakistan records establishing a documentation centre at Gor Khatri in 2010 for work on Peshawar's historic buildings. That is a modest but revealing continuation of institutional use: the complex became a setting for recording and understanding other parts of the city's heritage.

For a visitor, begin by reading the enclosure's organisation, then ask which elements belong to which uses and periods. The gateway, cell, religious structure and civic building need not compete for attention. Each answers a different question about travel, authority, devotion or administration.

Gor Khatri is most compelling when its layers remain intelligible together. Its story is not the replacement of one authentic past by a series of distractions. It is the repeated adaptation of a prominent urban place, with archaeology and architecture preserving different parts of that continuing history.

title: Sethi House and the merchant courtyard
summary: Sethi House connects the display of merchant wealth with the practical organisation of privacy, business and climate. Its courtyard is the hinge between those different demands.

body.text: The courtyard at Sethi House is more than a pleasant opening within a richly decorated building. It helps organise the relationship between reception, business, domestic life and movement through the house. In the dense fabric of old Peshawar, the residence turns inward without becoming disconnected from the commercial world that made it possible.

The federal archaeological catalogue associates the house with Seth Karim Bakhsh and records completion in 1884 after a long building campaign. Pakistan's 2026 Tentative List submission places it within Mohallah Sethian, close to major market routes, and describes it as both a family residence and a place of business. Those functions explain why its architecture must be read through access as well as ornament.
Who can move where?

The nomination describes stairways, screened corridors and service spaces that organised circulation while maintaining household privacy. A visitor entering today may follow a museum-style route that differs from historic patterns of movement. Doors and passages once helped distinguish the spaces available to a business visitor from those used by household members.

The courtyard provided a shared point of orientation without making all adjoining rooms equally public. This is an important distinction. An inward-facing plan can connect spaces visually while still controlling how they are reached. The arrangement allows proximity and separation to exist together.

The same submission identifies ventilated lower spaces and terraces among the house's responses to climate. Such features belong to the practical intelligence of the design. They should be studied alongside the decorative finish rather than treated as a less interesting technical background.
Light shaped by craft

The federal catalogue records carved entrance work, coloured glass in openings and decorated ceilings. These features change the experience of light and attention. A window is both an opening and a worked surface; a ceiling can become a field of pattern rather than a neutral cover above the room.

Look at how ornament is positioned. Does it emphasise a doorway, frame a view or concentrate attention in a reception space? Questions of placement help explain why craftsmanship matters architecturally. The value is not simply that expensive materials appear in large quantities, but that they participate in the organisation of a room.
One house in a larger merchant quarter

The Heritage Foundation's account of Peshawar conservation describes the Sethi neighbourhood as a wider group of merchant residences, some altered or lost. Its discussion of work on another property, Qadri Manzil, should not be silently transferred to Karim Bakhsh's house. Distinct buildings can share a neighbourhood history without sharing every date or repair campaign.

That wider context gives the surviving house added significance. A single carefully preserved interior cannot replace an entire historic residential fabric, but it can make the relationships between trade, family life and skilled work easier to understand.

At Sethi House, let the courtyard guide the visit. Follow the thresholds, notice changes in light and compare public-facing display with more contained spaces. The richness of the building lies in the way these practical and expressive decisions are brought together.

title: Shahbazgarhi: an inscription encountered in the landscape
summary: Shahbazgarhi’s two inscribed boulders show why a text’s physical arrangement matters. The separately carved twelfth edict also has a revealing history of nineteenth-century documentation.

body.text: At Shahbazgarhi, the arrangement of the text is part of the evidence. Ashoka's fourteen major edicts are distributed across two boulders rather than contained on one continuous surface. That physical separation once complicated their documentation and still invites a useful question: how does the placement of words affect the way a public message is encountered?

Pakistan's Tentative List description locates the inscriptions beside an old route connecting the Peshawar valley with northern valleys and Taxila. It dates them to the middle of the third century BCE and identifies Kharoshthi writing, read from right to left. The route, the rock and the script belong together in the interpretation.
The missing section that was nearby

Classicist Llewelyn Morgan, drawing on research undertaken with archaeologist Luca Olivieri, recounts a revealing episode in nineteenth-century scholarship. Charles Masson documented the principal inscription in 1838. Comparison with other versions showed that the twelfth edict was missing from the record. Harold Deane subsequently identified it on a separate nearby rock in 1888.

This was a change in scholarly documentation, not proof that local people had been unaware of the second boulder. The distinction matters whenever an archaeological account uses the language of discovery. What was new to a visiting recorder or a learned society was not necessarily new to the community around the site.

Morgan notes the separate treatment of the twelfth edict and discusses its emphasis on respect between religious groups. He offers the interpretation that this message may have had particular importance in the region. That is a historically informed reading of placement, not a fact explicitly explained by the rock's location alone.
Reading words and reading space

An edition that prints all fourteen edicts in sequence makes comparison easier, but it can conceal the physical experience of the originals. At Shahbazgarhi, moving between surfaces is part of encountering the text. Letter size, carving and separation can carry information that a plain transcription does not preserve.

The same principle applies to photographs. A tightly cropped image may help specialists examine letters while removing the inscription from its landscape. A wider record can show relationships between boulders and approaches but make the text illegible. Both forms of documentation have value because they answer different questions.
An imperial message, not a simple mirror of society

The edicts express a ruler's declared principles. They should not be treated as automatic proof that every subject followed those principles or that all religious relations were harmonious. The gap between a statement of intent and lived practice is itself a historical question.

For visitors, the most meaningful approach is to preserve the connection between text and place. Observe the boulders without touching or marking them, consult a reliable translation and notice how the words have been arranged. Shahbazgarhi's importance is not exhausted by its age. It also shows how political ideas were given a durable physical presence, and how careful documentation can recover details that a seemingly complete record once missed.

title: Bala Hisar Fort and Peshawar’s changing skyline
summary: Peshawar’s Bala Hisar is a repeatedly rebuilt fort whose prominence outlasts any one ruling period. Historical descriptions, surviving masonry and present institutional use need to be read separately.

body.text: Bala Hisar's position in Peshawar makes it a landmark even for people who never enter it. Its mass contributes to the city's skyline and provides a visible reminder that political authority has repeatedly occupied and reshaped prominent ground. The fort's history, however, cannot be reduced to a single surviving building from one ruling dynasty.

The federal archaeological catalogue describes repeated destruction and rebuilding through Mughal, Durrani, Sikh and British periods. It also preserves a historical description of Shah Shuja's residence, with an oblong court, water features and a raised setting for royal appearance. That account concerns an earlier arrangement; it should not be used as a literal description of every space visible today.
A place can outlast its architecture

The persistence of a fortified location does not mean its walls have remained unchanged. The catalogue records replacement of earthen walls with brick masonry under British rule. Such changes alter material, profile and construction while allowing the site's political and symbolic prominence to continue.

This is why an origin story and a building date are not the same thing. A reference to a fort in an early text may establish the importance of a location without dating a particular parapet or gateway. A careful architectural history asks which evidence belongs to the place, which to a structure and which to an episode of reconstruction.

The distinction is especially important because Bala Hisar is also the name of an archaeological mound at Charsadda. That is a separate site. Excavation accounts for the Charsadda mound should not be imported into the story of Peshawar's standing fortress simply because the names match.
A continuing institutional setting

Radio Pakistan's August 2026 report describes an organised university-student visit to Peshawar's fort, including its museum and a briefing by Frontier Corps Khyber Pakhtunkhwa North. A February 2025 report likewise records a planned educational tour. These establish documented visits, not a general guarantee of unrestricted public entry.

For anyone planning a visit, current access and photography arrangements require direct confirmation through the relevant local authorities. A photograph from an event, a social-media account or an old visitor schedule is not a reliable substitute. The fort remains part of a contemporary institutional setting rather than a neutral open-air ruin.
Seeing the fort from the city

The Peshawar Development Authority uses Bala Hisar as an identifiable city landmark. Its visibility is therefore part of the public experience even when internal access is limited. From permitted public viewpoints, the relationship between elevated enclosure and surrounding urban movement can be considered without intruding on controlled areas.

The strongest interpretation holds three histories apart but connected: the long importance of the location, the successive remaking of its architecture and its present use. Bala Hisar's authority in the skyline comes partly from that continuity of prominence, while its actual fabric reminds us that continuity is often produced through change.

title: Damb Sadaat and the archaeology of the Quetta valley
summary: Damb Sadaat places the Quetta valley within the archaeology of early regional communities. Its pottery, recorded excavations and wider comparisons help challenge a history focused only on the largest Indus cities.

body.text: The archaeology of early Pakistan is often narrated through a small number of great cities. Damb Sadaat, in the Quetta valley, invites a wider view. Its importance lies in the evidence of a regional settlement and in the comparisons that connect pottery, objects and building remains across a landscape larger than any one urban centre.

The Department of Archaeology's catalogue records a long history of investigation, including visits by Aurel Stein, later researchers and Walter Fairservis. It describes excavated pottery assemblages and structural evidence used to establish a sequence. The entry's chronological labels are not fully consistent, so they should not be compressed into a precise foundation date without returning to the excavation publications.
A regional research programme

The Penn Museum Archives' biographical account places Fairservis's work in the Quetta–Pishin valley in 1950–51 and identifies Damb Sadaat and Kili Ghul Mohammad among the sites he investigated. The American Museum of Natural History's publication record dates Excavations in the Quetta Valley to 1956. These records establish the history of research; they do not replace the detailed evidence in the excavation volume.

Thinking regionally changes the questions. Instead of asking only whether a settlement resembles Mohenjo Daro, we can ask how communities in the valley made objects, organised space and participated in exchange. Differences become evidence rather than deficiencies measured against a larger city.
Pottery as a relationship

A pottery assemblage is more than a collection of attractive painted fragments. Shape, fabric, decoration and manufacturing traces can be compared, while the deposits in which pieces occur establish their sequence. The relationship between these kinds of information matters: visual similarity alone does not prove that two sites were occupied at exactly the same moment.

Nor does a shared style automatically identify a single population. Vessels, skills and decorative ideas can move in different ways. A careful interpretation distinguishes the observation of resemblance from explanations involving trade, learning or migration. Those explanations require additional evidence.
Beyond one city-centred story

Jonathan Mark Kenoyer's account of the Indus tradition includes Damb Sadaat among regional sites yielding seals before the fully developed urban phase. He discusses such objects in relation to economic and social differentiation, while acknowledging the difficulty of measuring those differences archaeologically. This places the settlement within a broader discussion without making every seal proof of the same political system.

The contribution of a smaller site is therefore not limited to supplying a preliminary chapter before the famous cities appear. It can show local combinations of practices and materials that a city-centred narrative would miss.

For readers encountering Damb Sadaat through museum objects or excavation drawings rather than a visit, provenance is especially valuable. Ask which trench or phase an object belongs to and which comparisons support its interpretation. The site's significance grows through those recorded relationships: a regional community becomes part of a larger history without losing the particular evidence through which it is known.

title: Killi Gul Mohammad: what small excavations can reveal
summary: Killi Gul Mohammad demonstrates both the value and the limits of a small excavation sample. Its early settlement sequence is important, but absence from a narrow trench cannot establish absence from an entire community.

body.text: Killi Gul Mohammad is important not because every aspect of its early community has been recovered, but because a limited excavation revealed a sequence that helped frame larger questions. Near Quetta, the mound became part of twentieth-century research into settlement before the mature Indus cities. Its evidence also offers a clear lesson in archaeological sampling.

The federal catalogue places the site in the northern part of the Quetta valley, near the Quetta–Chaman route, and records excavation by Walter Fairservis in 1950–51. The Penn Museum Archives' account situates this work within his broader survey of the Quetta–Pishin region. A single trench belonged to a larger effort to understand how settlements related across the valley.
A deep view is not a wide view

In a discussion of early shell use, archaeologist Jonathan Mark Kenoyer describes Fairservis's excavation at Killi Gul Mohammad as a deep sondage: a restricted intervention designed to investigate the sequence below the surface. It revealed occupation extending from a phase without pottery into later periods with ceramics.

Such a trench can be highly informative about succession. It may show one deposit above another and allow changes in material to be studied through depth. Its limitation is spatial: the sampled area cannot reveal every activity that took place across the settlement.

Imagine investigating a modern neighbourhood through one narrow slice of ground. The sequence might be clear, but whether that slice crossed a kitchen, workshop, yard or passage would strongly affect the objects recovered. The same principle applies to an ancient mound, even when its surviving deposits are much more complex.
An absence that needs interpretation

Kenoyer notes that shell was not reported from the lower levels and was also absent from the published account of succeeding deposits. He cautions that the sample may not adequately represent the region's material culture. The observation is not a licence to invent missing objects; it is a reason to avoid an overly broad conclusion from a restricted sample.

“No shell was reported in this excavation” and “this community had no contact with shell materials” are different statements. The first describes an evidence base. The second proposes a historical explanation that would need wider support. Preserving the difference is one of archaeology's most useful habits.
Pottery and changing practice

The federal catalogue emphasises changes in pottery manufacture across the site's sequence. Those changes can be investigated through fabrics, forming methods, firing and decoration. They should not be turned into a simplistic ladder from primitive to advanced people. Different techniques answer different needs and may coexist.

Killi Gul Mohammad therefore contributes both substantive evidence and a lesson in how to use it. Its early sequence matters, while the limits of excavation remain part of every responsible account. For the reader, the most valuable question is not merely how old the mound is, but what was actually sampled and how that sample supports the story being told.

title: Nausharo between village and urban worlds
summary: Nausharo links regional Balochistan traditions with the Indus urban world through a sequence of buildings and objects. Its pottery and figurines reveal both connections and differences across time.

body.text: Nausharo is valuable because it complicates a clean dividing line between regional village traditions and an Indus urban world. The site preserves a sequence through which changes in architecture and material culture can be examined. Its significance is not that every phase looks the same, but that related and changing practices can be studied in their archaeological order.

The Department of Archaeology locates Nausharo in the Bolan plain of Kachhi and records four principal cultural periods. Its catalogue includes dwelling structures, painted pottery, human and animal figurines and Harappan seals among the evidence. This range allows questions about everyday activity and representation to sit beside those about wider cultural connections.
Sequence before labels

Jarrige, Didier and Quivron compare Nausharo's Harappan periods II, III and IV with sequences at other excavated sites. Such comparison is not simply a matter of matching famous names. It depends on relating material characteristics to stratigraphy and, where available, independent dating evidence.

A period label is a tool for organising evidence, not an event that every household experienced on the same day. Changes in vessels, buildings and other objects need not all occur together. A useful account therefore asks which practices continued, which changed and how securely those changes can be placed in time.

The authors also identify a minority component of material associated with the Oxus world in Nausharo's later Harappan period. That observation broadens the geographical discussion without requiring the whole settlement to be assigned a new identity. An assemblage can contain objects with different connections.
Figurines and local choices

Jonathan Mark Kenoyer's comparison of early art draws attention to greater variety among human figurines from Mehrgarh and Nausharo than in the Harappa material he discusses. He identifies applied clay decoration as an important technique at the Balochistan sites, contrasting it with other approaches visible at Harappa.

This comparison shows why resemblance and difference deserve equal attention. Shared participation in a wider tradition does not require identical visual habits. How a figure was formed or ornamented can carry evidence about learned practices and choices in making, even where the object's exact social or religious use remains uncertain.

Kenoyer presents further comparative study as a research opportunity. That phrasing should be retained rather than converted into a settled explanation of social identity. A human figurine is not automatically a goddess, a toy or a portrait; interpretation depends on context and a defensible argument.
A connected place with its own evidence

Nausharo helps replace a simple centre-and-periphery picture with a more demanding one. Regional communities could participate in broad networks while retaining particular techniques and histories. The task is to demonstrate those relationships through objects and deposits, not assume them from a map.

For readers, the best route into the site is to follow one class of evidence through its recorded sequence, then compare it with another. Pottery, figurines and architecture may tell overlapping but different stories. Together they make Nausharo an important place for understanding how cultural integration can occur alongside local continuity and change.
